run.market_summary: Three themes matter right now. (1) Chip export controls are the strongest and most-covered signal (score +0.69, news volume 8.4). The US has blocked China's remote access to AI chips, added license requirements for five countries and put curbs on Asian data centers. China has promised 'necessary measures', which puts the US-China trade truce at risk. Most of this is already in some prices: NVDA is down 12.6% in five days and SMH, AMAT and LRCX are each down about 5%. AMD is the clear laggard. (2) The Fed has turned hawkish. It raised rates for the first time since 2023, Musalem is calling for several more hikes by spring, and the dollar is at a 19-month high. That favors the dollar more than duration trades, because hikes could flatten the curve and safe-haven buying supports long bonds. (3) Iran is escalating again: a tanker was struck in Hormuz, Iran hit US targets in Bahrain for the third time after a two-month lull, and a third US carrier has arrived. Even so, crude fell over the week (USO -1.8%), squeezed by the strong dollar and hawkish Fed. That makes oil a short-term bet on further escalation, not a trend trade. Defense stocks and broad index shorts are weak, crowded ways to express these themes. Overall: a few trades, sized modestly.

ideas.thesis: The new US rules block China's remote access to advanced AI chips and require licenses for Asian data centers, which cuts into the AI accelerator market AMD is targeting. Yet AMD is down only 0.8% in five days, while NVDA is down 12.6% and SMH 5.2%. It is the cleanest name on this theme that hasn't moved yet.

The Fed's first hike since 2023, plus Musalem calling for several more hikes by spring, puts US rate policy at odds with other central banks. The dollar is already at a 19-month high and also gains from tariff escalation (50% tariffs on Canada) and safe-haven demand tied to Iran.

A tanker struck and disabled in Hormuz, Iran's third strike on US targets in Bahrain, and a third US carrier arriving all point to more supply risk. Crude has still fallen 1.8% this week, so oil is pricing little geopolitical premium if things escalate further. This is a small, short-term bet on escalation.

analysis.headline: Stocks fell across the board for a fourth straight session ahead of Nvidia's after-hours report. Only a few moves were unusual, all tied to specific news: UnitedHealth and other managed-care stocks fell on a proposed CMS anti-fraud audit rule, Nike reversed on its investor day, and the Dow took extra hits from Home Depot and JPMorgan. The selling grew during the session as tech gave up early gains.
analysis.narrative:
All 13 sector ETFs fell, the Dow lost about 849 points (-1.64%) and VIX rose 11%. Even so, few moves were statistically unusual. SPY's z was -0.7 and QQQ's -0.3. Macro assets barely moved: the 10-year yield fell 2bp to 5.10%, the dollar, gold and crude were flat, and TLT rose 0.2%. A day where bonds edge up and the dollar and gold sit still is not a macro shock. It looks like position-cutting before Nvidia's first report without Jensen Huang (options priced about an 8.5% move), with Anthropic's ~$1.4-1.5T IPO pricing Wednesday also pulling cash out of the market. Reuters quoted a strategist calling it general nervousness, not news on any one stock.

The gap and the session told different stories. Before the open, the Dow (-0.90% gap) and health care (-1.15%) were already down. Home Depot beat estimates but narrowed its EPS guidance, which CNBC said dragged Dow futures 200 points. UnitedHealth opened about 4.8% lower after CMS proposed the "CRUSH" anti-fraud rule, which would extrapolate Medicare Advantage audit findings back to payment year 2018. Humana fell about 4.4% and ELV and MOH about 2%. Tech and semis opened higher (XLK +0.36%, SMH +0.98%, NVDA +0.5%) after Huang said he was open to returning. All of that faded during the session: XLK -1.26% and SMH -1.36% from the open. Software led the drop (CRM -8.5%, INTU -5.4%, WDAY -4.8%, MSFT -2.3%). Kiplinger also tied part of the tech weakness to a reported outage of the NSA's classified network, coming after bank outages on Monday.

Financials (XLF -1.89%, KRE -1.86%, volume 1.6x) were the weakest large sector. JPMorgan fell 2.5% after naming insider Bregje de Best as its next CFO. Berkshire's 13F showed another 5.7% cut to its Bank of America stake. Headlines also noted that the KBW bank index is close to a 'death cross' (its 50-day average falling below its 200-day). Nike was the clearest single-stock story. It opened 5% higher on long-term (2029) growth targets, then fell 10.8% from the open once management called FY28 'challenging financially' and pointed to weakness in China. Utilities had the most unusual sector move (z -2.0) even though yields fell, so rates don't explain it. Data released during the session was mixed: retail sales were strong, industrial production was weak, and homebuilder sentiment fell to its lowest since April 2012. None of it moved yields much.

analysis.cross_asset_read: Stocks fell broadly but other markets stayed calm. The 10-year fell only 2bp (5.10%), TLT rose 0.2%, and the dollar, gold and crude were all flat. VIX rose 11% from a level already up about 31% on the week. This was equity de-risking before a binary event (NVDA) plus specific news (CMS rule, Nike, HD, JPM), not a macro repricing. Rates did not drive it: growth stocks fell while yields eased, and defensive sectors such as XLU, XLP and XLV fell more than tech. Oil holding flat while Iran threats continued, with RTX and NOC up during the session, shows only a small geopolitical bid. December hike odds held at about 95%. Today's data (strong retail sales, weak industrial production, NAHB at its lowest since 2012) did not move the front of the curve.

axis_realized.note: CMS CRUSH Medicare Advantage audit rule: UNH -5.4% (z -3.6), HUM -4.4%, XLV gapped -1.15%

Homebuilder sentiment hit its lowest since 2012 and industrial production was weak, but retail sales were strong. Small effect: IWM -1.4%, yields barely down

model_grade.summary: The model's top theme (chip export controls) did not drive US prices today: semis opened higher and the later drop was about NVDA earnings. Its hawkish-Fed and Iran themes produced flat prices. The three trade ideas gained only because the market fell, not because their theses played out. It missed the actual drivers: the CMS managed-care rule, the pre-NVDA de-risking, and stock-specific news at Nike, Home Depot and JPMorgan.
got_right: Chip export controls did weigh on Chinese tech (BABA -4.4%, KWEB -2.1%), in line with its 'US-China truce at risk' framing
Its summary said broad index shorts were crowded and weak ways to express these themes. Indexes fell, but only about 1 standard deviation, consistent with no clean theme trade
LONG UUP and LONG USO beat SPY by roughly 1%, but only because both were flat while stocks fell
got_wrong: Chip export controls at +0.69 as the strongest signal: US semis opened +1% (SMH, NVDA up) and the session drop was about NVDA earnings and software, not new controls
SHORT AMD: AMD rose 0.17% and beat SPY. It did not catch up to NVDA's losses
Hawkish monetary policy at +0.42: the 10-year fell 2bp, TLT rose and the dollar was flat. Policy did not reprice today
Geopolitical/energy at +0.49/+0.31: crude was flat (-0.09%) and gold flat. Iran threats were not priced
missed: CMS CRUSH Medicare Advantage rule (healthcare_policy), today's largest unusual move (UNH z -3.6, XLV gap -1.15%)
Nvidia earnings and Anthropic IPO as the main reasons investors cut risk
Home Depot guidance narrowing hitting the Dow before the open
Bank weakness (JPM CFO, Berkshire BAC sale, death-cross technicals, outage headlines) and the software selloff (CRM -8.5%)

lessons: Add a scheduled-event check: when a mega-cap report like NVDA or a mega-IPO is due the same day, expect broad de-risking and lower conviction on theme trades. Don't size chip-policy shorts into a binary earnings print

When a theme has dominated news for more than 24 hours and the related stocks already fell hard (NVDA -12.6% over 5 days), cut its score for the next session. A large share of headlines means it's priced in, not that a new move is coming
Scan regulatory dockets (CMS, FDA, HHS proposed rules) before the open. Healthcare_policy was missing from the theme scores even though it drove the largest unusual move
Add a check for Dow-specific premarket earnings (HD, UNH, JPM). A DIA gap much larger than SPY's points to price-weighted single-stock news
Judge long-USD and long-oil ideas on absolute return, not just versus SPY. On risk-off days they 'win' relatively without the thesis working
